articles.title: Heywood nursery loses planning bid to keep caravan as outbuilding
articles.excerpt: Little Oaks Nursery in Heywood has been denied permission to retain a caravan used as an outbuilding, following a planning decision by Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
Little Oaks Nursery, located on Bamford Road in Heywood, has lost its bid to keep a caravan that replaced a temporary Portakabin in its yard. The nursery applied for retrospective planning permission for the caravan, which has been used as an outbuilding since the Portakabin was removed in 2024 after being granted temporary permission in 2022.

A report from a planning officer indicated that pre-application advice had been sought regarding the placement of a static caravan on the site. The advice stated that such a structure would not be visually appropriate and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. Despite this, the caravan was placed on the site without the necessary planning permission, prompting the nursery's application to regulate its presence.

The planning officer's report further noted that the caravan does not meet the high-quality design standards required for a permanent structure. It was concluded that the caravan does not offer any visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaced, which was only accepted for a limited time due to its unsuitability for permanent retention.

This decision by Rochdale Council highlights ongoing concerns regarding planning regulations and the visual impact of structures within the area. Local residents and businesses may be affected by the enforcement of these regulations, as they aim to maintain the aesthetic integrity of the neighbourhood.

articles.title: New documentary explores the history of Hollingworth Lake
articles.excerpt: A new YouTube documentary delves into the fascinating history of Hollingworth Lake, revealing its origins and significance to the local community.
articles.content_html:
Hollingworth Lake, a popular recreational area for residents of Oldham, Rochdale, and surrounding regions, has been the subject of a new YouTube documentary that explores its intriguing history. Created by Malc Grimwood, a local history enthusiast, the documentary is part of his channel "Tales From Trails Around The Dales."

The lake, situated on the outskirts of Littleborough beneath the Pennine hills, is a man-made body of water that was established during the Industrial Revolution to support the extensive canal network. Grimwood highlights the lake's significance, stating, "Hollingworth Lake is one of Rochdale's most cherished and well-known beauty spots, offering an escape and a place to enjoy its open spaces and rural setting."

The documentary not only sheds light on the lake's origins but also aims to connect viewers with the natural beauty and historical context of the area. It showcases the surrounding countryside, wooded slopes, and moorland that contribute to the lake's charm and appeal.

For those interested in local history and the environment, the documentary serves as an engaging resource. It invites viewers to appreciate the rich heritage of Hollingworth Lake and encourages them to explore the area, fostering a deeper connection with this beloved landmark.

articles.title: Rochdale Council encourages reporting of concerns regarding HMOs
articles.excerpt: Residents are urged to report any issues with Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) to ensure tenant safety and compliance with regulations.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is urging residents to report any concerns related to Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs). This initiative aims to protect tenants from inappropriate and illegal behaviour by landlords, ensuring that living conditions meet safety standards.

Residents can report issues through the council's dedicated webpage, which provides contact details and access to the licensing register for HMOs. The council has a legal obligation to address concerns and maintain housing standards in the borough.

The number of HMOs has been increasing in Rochdale, raising concerns about tenant safety and compliance with housing regulations. By reporting issues, residents can assist the council in taking appropriate action against non-compliant landlords.

For more information or to report a concern, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council's website or email housing.standards@rochdale.gov.uk.

articles.title: Weather warning issued for Rochdale as Storm Boelo approaches
articles.excerpt: Residents in Rochdale are advised to prepare for potential disruption as Storm Boelo is expected to bring strong winds and heavy rain this weekend.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Rochdale are being warned to prepare for disruption as Storm Boelo approaches the borough this afternoon. The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for wind, predicting strong gusts that could cause damage to buildings and trees, as well as affecting local rivers and roads.

Forecasters expect Storm Boelo to bring a very windy and wet spell this weekend, with strong winds spreading across northern parts of the UK on Saturday afternoon. Gusts of 55-65 mph are likely widely, with some coastal and exposed areas potentially experiencing gusts of 70-80 mph or more, particularly in Scotland and the far north of England.

The storm follows closely on the heels of Storm Austen, which recently impacted the south, south-west, and parts of Wales, with winds reaching up to 84 mph. Residents are encouraged to stay updated on weather conditions and take necessary precautions to ensure their safety during the storm's passage.

As Storm Boelo is expected to persist overnight and through much of Sunday, it is crucial for local residents to remain vigilant and prepared for possible disruptions. This weather event highlights the importance of being aware of severe weather warnings and taking proactive measures to protect homes and property.

articles.title: Decision on 450-home development in Bamford delayed again
articles.excerpt: The planning committee has deferred a decision on a housing scheme in Bamford, citing insufficient drainage details and historical flooding issues.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale planning committee has once again delayed a decision on a proposed housing development in Bamford, which aims to build 45 homes as part of a larger 450-home project. The committee's latest meeting on October 22 revealed ongoing concerns about drainage and flooding on the site, which is located behind Greenvale.

In August, the committee had previously deferred the application from Wain Homes, expressing the need for more detailed plans to address historic drainage issues. Councillors noted that without a comprehensive masterplan for the entire development, they could not make an informed decision. The site, which was removed from green belt status under the Greater Manchester housing strategy, has been flagged for its seasonal flooding problems.

Objector Lisa Bailey highlighted the site's history of flooding, stating that the area is 'seasonally wet ground'. She urged the committee to ensure that infrastructure and access issues are adequately addressed before any development proceeds. Coun Stephen Anstee remarked on the unusually high number of conditions attached to the application, indicating that the proposal is not yet ready for approval.

Wain Homes' planning agent, Stephen Harris, argued that a flood risk management assessment was included in their application and that the other developers involved in the wider scheme had no objections. However, the committee decided to defer the application again, requesting a full report on drainage management from Wain Homes before proceeding.

articles.title: Rochdale wins gold at Britain in Bloom awards, crowned champion
articles.excerpt: Rochdale has been awarded gold at this year’s Britain in Bloom awards, securing the title of overall winner in the Town Centres and City Centres category.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has achieved a remarkable victory by winning gold at this year’s Britain in Bloom awards, being crowned the overall champion in the Town Centres and City Centres category. This accolade places Rochdale ahead of competitors such as Floral Godalming from the Southeast and Shaftesbury in Bloom from the South, as well as Sidcup Partners Limited from London.

The town's success in this prestigious competition is a continuation of its strong performance in recent years, having previously secured gold in 2018 and being named Best Small City in 2022. Last year, Middleton town centre held the title, making this win particularly significant as it keeps the award within the borough.

Judges praised Rochdale for its vibrant floral displays, which were provided by Bowlee Garden Nursery, as well as its recycling initiatives and exceptional cleanliness. They highlighted the pride, teamwork, and dedication of the community, along with the commitment to local biodiversity and strong partnerships that exceeded the gold standard in horticulture and environmental responsibility.

Rochdale's historic Baillie Street Quarter and the striking murals created during the 2025 Rochdale Common Walls Festival were also noted for showcasing the town's culture and civic pride. This recognition not only celebrates the town's beauty but also reflects the ongoing regeneration efforts supported by a multi-million-pound National Lottery Heritage Fund grant.

articles.title: New HMO licensing requirements introduced by Rochdale Borough Council
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced new licensing requirements for Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs), aimed at ensuring safety and compliance among landlords.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has introduced new licensing requirements for landlords operating Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) within the borough. This initiative is part of the council's ongoing efforts to ensure that all rental properties meet safety and compliance standards, thereby protecting tenants and the wider community.

Under the new regulations, landlords must obtain a specific HMO licence for each property they manage. The licence is valid for five years, with a fee of £1,011 plus an additional £53 inspection fee per habitable room. This means that landlords with multiple properties will need to apply for a separate licence for each one, ensuring that all HMOs are properly regulated.

The council will conduct thorough checks to determine if landlords are 'fit and proper persons' to manage these properties. This may include a Disclosure and Barring Service check if initial assessments raise concerns. The licensing process aims to enhance the safety and living conditions for tenants residing in HMOs across Rochdale.

These changes are significant for both landlords and tenants in the area. articles.title: Inspector rejects garden fence appeal on Town House Road, Littleborough
articles.excerpt: A planning inspector has upheld Rochdale Council's decision to refuse retrospective planning permission for a garden fence at 19 Town House Road, Littleborough, citing its negative impact on the area's character.
articles.content_html:
A planning inspector has ruled against a homeowner's appeal regarding a garden fence at 19 Town House Road, Littleborough. Caterina Buonocore had sought retrospective planning permission for a 1.55-metre high boundary fence, which is approximately twice the height of the original fence. The council had previously rejected her application, leading to the appeal.

In the inspector's decision, it was stated that the main concern was the fence's effect on the character and appearance of the area. The inspector noted that boundary treatments in the locality are typically low-level and visually permeable, contributing to a sense of openness and allowing the greenery in front gardens to be appreciated. The inspector remarked that the existing vegetation helps to soften the street scene, enhancing the area's character.

The inspector further explained that the close-boarded timber fence introduced by the appeal contrasts sharply with the more traditional forms of boundary treatment found in the neighbourhood. Observations made on-site indicated that, due to the prominent corner location, the fence appeared particularly stark and incongruous against the backdrop of traditional stone terraces with lower boundary treatments.

As a result of this ruling, Buonocore may now be required to remove the fence, which could have implications for her property and the surrounding area. The decision underscores the importance of maintaining the character of local neighbourhoods and adhering to planning regulations.

articles.title: Plans for 45-home development in Bamford face over 300 objections
articles.excerpt: More than 300 objections have been lodged against plans to demolish a house in Bamford to make way for a new 45-home development, which is recommended for approval by Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
Plans to demolish a house in Bamford to facilitate a new 45-home development have sparked significant local opposition, with over 300 objections submitted to Rochdale Council. The proposal, submitted by Wain Homes, involves the demolition of 58 Greenvale, known as Chadwick Farm Barn, to create access to the new housing development planned for land south of the property.

The proposed development includes 39 homes for market sale, comprising 14 three-bedroom, seven four-bedroom, and 18 five-bedroom houses, along with six homes designated for social housing. The council's planning committee is set to review the application on Thursday, following a deferral in August due to concerns regarding the absence of a comprehensive housing masterplan.

Local residents have raised multiple concerns regarding the development, including the premature release of the site, inadequacies in local infrastructure, highway capacity and road safety issues, as well as potential drainage and flooding problems. Additionally, objections highlight the impact on local ecology and landscape, and the effects on the amenity of existing residents.

The planning application comes in the wake of a revised National Planning Policy Framework aimed at boosting housing supply and economic growth. As the council prepares to make a decision, the significant number of objections may influence the outcome of the proposal.

articles.title: 651 SEWAGE SPILLS INTO THE RIVER ROCH: 3,271 HOURS OF DISCHARGES — WHAT IS IN OUR WATER AND WHO PAYS?
articles.excerpt: Seventeen outlets discharged into the River Roch in 2025. Rochdale Daily examines what residents and wildlife may be exposed to, how water is tested, why storm overflows operate, and which fines have actually been imposed.
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

The River Roch received 651 recorded storm-overflow discharges during 2025, lasting a combined 3,271 hours across 17 outlets, according to the environmental data project Top of the Poops, drawing on water-company returns submitted to the Environment Agency. Two further outlets listed in the same river table reported no discharges. Every identified operator was United Utilities.

The numbers are startling, but require careful interpretation. The 3,271 hours are added together across outlets; some will have run simultaneously. It does not mean the whole river was continuously receiving discharges for 3,271 hours. Neither the duration monitors nor the count establish the volume released, chemical or bacterial concentrations, any particular person's illness, or whether an individual discharge was unlawful.

Sources: Top of the Poops, River Roch 2025 monitoring summary, https://www.top-of-the-poops.org/waterway/united-utilities/river-roch; Environment Agency, 2025 national storm overflow annual returns, https://www.data.gov.uk/dataset/19f6064d-7356-466f-844e-d20ea10ae9fd/event-duration-monitoring-storm-overflows-annual-returns

WHERE DID THE SEWAGE ENTER?

Rochdale wastewater treatment works recorded 104 spills lasting approximately 1,503 hours — around 46% of the 3,271 combined hours. Oakenrod combined sewer overflow recorded 87 events lasting approximately 508 hours. At Heywood (Botany) treatment works the figures were 35 events and 240 hours; Sudden Valley sewer recorded 83 events and 235 hours.

Other identified outlets included Smith Bridge Road (20 events, 158 hours), Hooley Bridge (39, 140), Albert Royds Street (73, 138), Peel Lane No. 1 (43, 92) and Peel Lane No. 2 (35, 69). These outlets are along different stretches of the river and should not all be described as being in the town centre.

Figures: https://www.top-of-the-poops.org/waterway/united-utilities/river-roch

WHY DOES THIS HAPPEN? MOST ARE NOT BURST PIPES

Much of the North West uses combined sewers, carrying rainwater from roofs and roads in the same pipes as foul sewage from toilets, bathrooms and businesses. During heavy rainfall or snowmelt, the combined flow can exceed sewer and treatment capacity. Storm overflows act as designed pressure-release points, allowing diluted, often untreated sewage and rainwater into rivers rather than letting the system back up into homes. At treatment works, storm tanks store surplus flows, but may overflow when capacity is exceeded.

That explains how the infrastructure is intended to work; it does not establish that all 651 individual River Roch operations were authorised. Legal discharge depends on the actual permit, flow thresholds and conditions at the time. Equipment failure, maintenance problems, insufficient capacity or inappropriate operation can also lead to pollution breaches. It would take rainfall, flow-to-full-treatment, maintenance and permit records to determine the reason and legality of each event.

United Utilities has said that 54% of its North West sewerage network is combined, and describes plans for further capacity and rainwater separation. The Environment Agency says longstanding underinvestment and poor asset maintenance contribute to high national overflow usage. These are wider explanations, not documented causes assigned individually to each River Roch spill.

Sources: Environment Agency, what storm overflow monitors show, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/fewer-and-shorter-storm-overflow-spills-in-2025-new-monitoring-data-shows; United Utilities better rivers report, https://www.unitedutilities.com/globalassets/documents/pdf/united-utilities-better-rivers-report-2024.pdf; Environment Agency explanation, https://environmentagency.blog.gov.uk/2025/03/27/what-are-the-2024-edm-annual-returns/

WHAT DOES 'MEASURING WATER QUALITY' ACTUALLY MEAN?

Event Duration Monitors (EDMs) measure WHEN an overflow runs and HOW LONG it runs; they do not measure the litres discharged, how much faecal bacteria is present, the ammonia concentration, or whether water is safe for people to enter. National spill counts use the regulatory event-counting methodology, rather than equalling every individual sensor activation.

River health is assessed separately through Environment Agency sampling, ecological surveys and modelling. Measurements can include dissolved oxygen, ammonia, phosphate, biological oxygen demand, temperature, acidity (pH) and selected chemical contaminants. Ecologists also survey fish, invertebrates and water plants, and consider habitat modification. An overall ecological classification combines several measures, so improvement in one chemical does not automatically mean the whole river is healthy.

For designated bathing waters, officials specifically test E. coli and intestinal enterococci as indicators of faecal contamination. Ordinary rivers are not necessarily sampled for those bacteria as regular bathing-water sites. No verified River Roch-wide 2025 bacteria sampling series has been identified in the sources examined. An overflow monitor cannot be used as a certificate of safe swimming water.

Sources: Environment Agency, river classification framework, https://engageenvironmentagency.uk.engagementhq.com/understanding-englands-water-environment/widgets/155553/faqs; Environment Agency, bathing-water bacteria testing, https://environmentagency.blog.gov.uk/2025/05/15/how-the-environment-agency-monitors-and-tests-bathing-water-quality/

WHAT DO THE RIVER'S ACTUAL TESTS SHOW?

There is documented progress as well as continuing concern. In August 2026 the Environment Agency reported that phosphate quality on the River Roch (Spodden to Irwell) improved from POOR in 2019 to GOOD in the 2025 classification. It attributed the improvement to treatment upgrades and a catchment-wide permitting system requiring better phosphorus removal at wastewater treatment works. That is an important environmental gain.

However, the Environment Agency's catchment records classify the lower Roch waterbody's ecological status as MODERATE in its published records: invertebrates were moderate and aquatic macrophytes (larger water plants) poor in the 2022 assessment. The source-to-Spodden waterbody also had moderate ecological status in the recorded classification. These classifications describe river condition, not evidence that the 2025 overflows caused each shortcoming. Historical chemical failures include persistent contaminants with multiple potential sources.

Sources: Environment Agency, August 2026 reporting, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/new-data-to-drive-action-to-improve-englands-rivers-and-lakes; Environment Agency lower River Roch waterbody, https://environment.data.gov.uk/catchment-planning/WaterBody/GB112069064600; upper River Roch waterbody, https://environment.data.gov.uk/catchment-planning/WaterBody/GB112069064720

HOW MIGHT PEOPLE AND PETS BE AFFECTED?

Untreated sewage-contaminated water can contain bacteria, viruses and parasites. Exposure while swimming, paddling, retrieving a ball or handling contaminated riverbank material can increase the risk of stomach illness, skin, eye or ear infection and, in some circumstances, severe infections. Risks depend on the actual organisms and concentration, exposure route and the person involved. The monitoring totals do not show that residents of Rochdale have been made ill by any specific spill.

Children and dog walkers using the riverbank should not mistake clear-looking water or a 'not currently spilling' monitor for proof of safety. Avoid swallowing untreated river water, wash hands after contact, keep pets from drinking discoloured or foul-smelling water, and keep children away from visible sewage contamination. Contact with the river is a different issue from the quality of treated drinking water delivered to household taps: these overflow figures do NOT show that Rochdale's tap water is contaminated.

Source: UKHSA/Environment Agency open-water health guidance, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/swim-healthy-leaflet/swim-healthy

WHAT HAPPENS TO FISH, INSECTS AND WILDLIFE?

Sewage carries organic matter and nutrients. As microorganisms break down the waste, dissolved oxygen can fall, stressing fish and aquatic insects. Ammonia can be directly toxic to fish and invertebrates at sufficiently high concentrations; excessive nutrients can encourage algal growth and alter plant communities. Repeated pulses can affect sensitive species even where a river looks normal between storms.

The River Roch's invertebrate and plant classifications warrant continued scrutiny, but attribution matters: modified channels, urban runoff, other pollution and long-lived chemicals also affect ecological health. This investigation found no verified evidence that 651 measured overflow events killed a specified number of fish or animals in the Roch in 2025. The proper test would combine event timing with upstream/downstream sampling and evidence of wildlife impacts.

Source: Environment Agency evidence of ammonia and fish mortality in a separate investigated river pollution case, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/anglian-water-fined-300-000-after-pollution-killed-5-000-fish; River Roch classification, https://environment.data.gov.uk/catchment-planning/WaterBody/GB112069064600

IS THE RIVER GETTING BETTER?

At Rochdale wastewater treatment works, recorded overflow events fell from 116 in 2024 to 104 in 2025; discharge hours fell from approximately 1,679 to 1,503. Oakenrod likewise fell from 101 spills and around 662 hours in 2024 to 87 spills and around 508 hours in 2025. These are improvements in recorded overflow frequency and duration at those sites — NOT proof that concentrations of pathogens or total sewage volumes fell by the same proportions.

Across England, storm-overflow events fell by 35% and monitored spill duration fell by 48% in 2025 compared with 2024. The Environment Agency emphasises that 2025 was unusually dry, so these comparisons cannot all be attributed to improved infrastructure.

Sources: Rochdale works historical spill data, https://sewagemap.org.uk/locations/rochdale-wwtw; Oakenrod historical spill data, https://sewagemap.org.uk/locations/oakenrod-cso; Environment Agency national 2025 figures, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/fewer-and-shorter-storm-overflow-spills-in-2025-new-monitoring-data-shows

IS UNITED UTILITIES FINED FOR SEWAGE DISCHARGES?

Yes, when regulators establish breaches. The Environment Agency can investigate permit breaches and prosecute serious offences. Courts determine criminal fines, while other cases may be resolved through environmental enforcement undertakings and restoration payments. But discharging from a permitted storm overflow during qualifying conditions is not automatically a criminal offence, and a published spill count is NOT a count of proved illegal discharges.

On 8 September 2026 United Utilities was fined £900,000, plus £62,225 prosecution costs and a £2,000 surcharge, after admitting five environmental permit offences over sewage discharges on the FYLDE COAST following a pipe failure in 2023. In a separate case, United Utilities agreed a £517,000 environmental enforcement undertaking following permit breaches affecting the RIVER TAME in Tameside. Neither was a fine for these 651 River Roch events.

Ofwat opened an enforcement case into United Utilities' wider wastewater operations in July 2024. As of the regulator's latest published investigation-status page, that case remains OPEN; opening a case is not a finding that particular River Roch spills were illegal.

Crucially, Rochdale Daily has not identified a published fine or formal penalty specifically attributable to the 651 River Roch discharges in 2025. That is NOT a finding that no breaches occurred: the Environment Agency must be asked for inspection, incident and enforcement records for each relevant permit.

Sources: Environment Agency Fylde conviction, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/water-company-fined-record-900k-after-coastline-sewage-spill; River Tame payment, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/environment-agency-secures500k-for-tame-catchment-improvements; Ofwat enforcement status, https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/investigation-into-sewage-treatment-works-and-networks/

WHEN WILL IT STOP?

United Utilities says it plans to invest more than £3 billion in storm-overflow improvements across the North West, targeting a 60% reduction in spills over the decade to 2030. In December 2025 it also announced a £4.5 million storage project at CASTLETON treatment works, expected to complete by the end of 2026 — but that scheme concerns Trub Brook and the River Irk, NOT the River Roch outlets in the 651 tally.

For meaningful local accountability, United Utilities should provide a dated, outlet-by-outlet plan for Rochdale wastewater treatment works, Oakenrod, Sudden Valley and the other River Roch overflows, with construction milestones, budgets, expected reductions and results after completion.

Sources: United Utilities investment strategy, https://corporate.unitedutilities.com/better-rivers/; Castleton project announcement, https://www.unitedutilities.com/corporate/newsroom/latest-news/united-utilities-starts-4.5m-scheme-in-castleton/

QUESTIONS FOR UNITED UTILITIES AND THE ENVIRONMENT AGENCY

Rochdale Daily is asking: (1) Of the 651 recorded River Roch events in 2025, how many were checked against rainfall and permit limits, and were any found to be unauthorised? (2) What were the estimated discharge volumes and upstream/downstream E. coli, enterococci, ammonia and dissolved-oxygen measurements near Rochdale works and Oakenrod? (3) What fish kills, wildlife incidents or public health complaints have been linked by regulators to the relevant outlets? (4) Which sites were inspected and what warnings, civil penalties, enforcement undertakings or prosecutions resulted? (5) Exactly which River Roch upgrades have been funded, when will they be completed and how will the effect be measured?

Residents witnessing suspected sewage or dead fish can report water pollution to the Environment Agency's 24-hour hotline, 0800 80 70 60, or its online report-water-pollution service. Note the date, location, smell, colour and any visible debris; do not enter dangerous water to gather evidence.

Source: https://www.gov.uk/report-water-pollution

THE BOTTOM LINE

Six hundred and fifty-one recorded sewage discharges are an important indicator of pressure on the River Roch's sewerage system, not 651 proven crimes. There is measurable progress in phosphate and at some monitored sites; there is also a compelling need for bacteriological data, permit compliance evidence and outlet-level investment results. Residents deserve those answers before being told the river is either safe or beyond recovery.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to consider motion to reassess climate targets amid cost-of-living crisis
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will discuss a motion from Cllr John Taylor on 13 October, urging a shift in focus from climate targets to addressing the cost-of-living crisis affecting residents.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to discuss a motion on 13 October that calls for a reassessment of its climate emergency targets in light of the ongoing cost-of-living crisis. The motion, proposed by Councillor John Taylor, suggests that the council prioritise immediate support for residents over its commitment to environmental goals.

In 2019, the council declared a climate emergency and pledged to achieve carbon neutrality by 2038. However, Cllr Taylor argues that the local impact on carbon reduction has been minimal and that resources could be better allocated to address pressing economic challenges faced by the community.

The council meeting will also include updates on initiatives such as the expansion of the electric vehicle charging network and the Rochdale Town Centre Heat Network, which aims to utilise heat from sewers to reduce energy costs for buildings. The council has received a £1 million grant from the Government to support this project and will soon begin seeking a development partner.

As the council considers this motion, residents may be interested in how these discussions could influence future policies and support measures during the current economic climate.

articles.title: Syke granted Conservation Area status to protect its historic character
articles.excerpt: Syke has been granted Conservation Area status by Rochdale Borough Council, following a consultation in which 33 of 38 responses supported the designation.
articles.content_html:
Syke has been granted Conservation Area status by Rochdale Borough Council, with the designation intended to protect the area's architectural and historic character from unsympathetic development.

The council confirmed the designation on 17 February 2026, describing Syke as an area with a unique and rich history. It highlighted the area's position on a historic packhorse route and its traditional weavers' cottages, including buildings with distinctive upper-floor windows designed to maximise natural light before electricity became widespread.

The Syke Conservation Area Appraisal provides further historical detail. It identifies Syke Road as part of the historic packhorse route linking Clitheroe with Rochdale and beyond, and records a network of historic paths across the Common, including remnants of the old packhorse trail.

The designated area covers Syke Common, parts of Dewhirst Road and Syke Road, and sections of Buckley Wood. The appraisal also identifies the northern extent of Cronkeyshaw Common and Syke Pond, well-preserved weavers' cottages, evidence of former industry, vernacular buildings and farmsteads, sandstone buildings, dry-stone and flagstone walls, and historic views and paths.

The appraisal includes historic maps from 1851, 1891, 1911 and 1936, alongside sections covering architectural character, historic buildings, key views and vistas, green spaces and the area's overall character. It provides the documented basis for the council's assessment of Syke's special architectural and historic interest.

### Public support for the designation

Rochdale Borough Council said more than 85% of locals backed the proposals. The consultation records 38 responses, of which 33 were positive about Conservation Area status for Syke. That represents approximately 87% of respondents, although the total number of responses was relatively small.

The responses nevertheless provide evidence of strong support among those who took part, as well as an indication that local heritage was an important consideration for respondents.

Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for regeneration, described the designation as a worthy addition to Rochdale's existing Conservation Areas and highlighted local engagement and pride in Syke's heritage.

### What Conservation Area status means

Conservation Areas are designated by local authorities where an area has special architectural or historic interest. Historic England guidance also provides for local authorities to prepare Conservation Area Appraisals setting out an area's character and significance.

The Syke appraisal states that its purpose is to explain the area's significance and identify measures to preserve and enhance its special character. It is intended to guide future development and inform future management plans. The document was prepared following consultation with local residents and draws on site visits, archive material, information from residents and Historic England guidance.

Historic England told Rochdale Daily that it had no involvement in the designation of the new Syke Conservation Area and directed us to its general guidance on Conservation Areas. Council documents show that Historic England guidance and documentation were considered during the process, but the designation itself was determined locally.

### Planning protections and what is not yet established

Conservation Area status introduces additional considerations within the planning process and can make permitted development rights more restrictive. The appraisal identifies circumstances where planning permission may be required, including substantial demolition of buildings or structures and certain works involving walls, gates, fences, extensions and alterations.

Article 4 Directions can remove further permitted development rights, but they are not automatic consequences of Conservation Area designation. The available information does not establish that an Article 4 Direction has been introduced for Syke.

The practical effect on individual properties will therefore depend on the planning controls that apply and any further decisions made by Rochdale Borough Council. The designation provides a framework for protecting Syke's special character, while the appraisal sets out the evidence and management considerations underpinning it.

articles.title: Wildfire emergency alert: an overreaction, or a sign of things to come?
articles.excerpt: Millions of phones across England and Wales sounded a Government Emergency Alert as wildfire risk reached exceptional levels. Was the intrusive warning proportionate, or are Britons being introduced to a hazard we will increasingly have to live with?
articles.content_html:
Millions of mobile phones across England and Wales emitted the unmistakable siren of the Government's Emergency Alerts system on Friday evening, carrying a warning about the risk of wildfires during exceptionally hot and dry conditions. People were urged not to light barbecues, campfires, bonfires or fireworks and to call 999 if they saw a fire.

For many people in Rochdale, where there was no wall of flame approaching their homes and no instruction to evacuate, the reaction was understandable: was this really what the country's most intrusive public-warning system was designed for? Emergency Alerts override ordinary phone settings and make a deliberately alarming noise intended to make people stop what they are doing immediately. Until recently, many people probably imagined receiving one only where there was a direct and imminent threat to life.

That makes the question worth asking. Was Friday's warning an overreaction, or was it an indication of how Britain's relationship with extreme weather is changing?

There is a reasonable argument that the Government must be careful not to overuse the system. Emergency warnings derive much of their effectiveness from their rarity. If people become accustomed to the siren being used for preventative advice that could have been distributed through television, radio, ordinary text messages and social media, warning fatigue becomes a real concern. A person who concludes that the alerts are unnecessarily dramatic may disable them and then miss a genuinely local warning about rapidly rising floodwater, an industrial accident or a fire approaching their home.

The Government should therefore be prepared to explain why this particular threshold was met and why an alert covering England and Wales was considered preferable to narrower regional warnings. Public confidence in an emergency system depends partly upon people understanding why its most intrusive warning mechanism has been activated.

However, dismissing the warning as hysteria would ignore the extraordinary situation confronting fire and rescue services this summer. Britain has experienced a succession of major wildfires during prolonged heat and drought. By Friday, national reporting indicated that the number of wildfires in England and Wales had already exceeded the 1,017 recorded during 2025, itself a record year. Dozens of fires were active around the country, major incidents had been declared, homes had been destroyed in the West Midlands and military personnel were being deployed to assist overstretched emergency services.

That changes the context considerably. Friday's message was not sent because somebody in Whitehall had suddenly discovered that dry grass can burn. It arrived during an active national wildfire emergency in which firefighters were already dealing with the consequences of repeated ignition in exceptionally dry landscapes.

The important distinction is between the probability of a fire starting and the severity of what may happen once one starts. Fire-danger measures do not necessarily predict that a particular patch of moorland will ignite. They indicate how easily vegetation may burn and how difficult a fire could become to control if ignition occurs. During ordinary British weather, carelessly discarded heat may produce a small scorched area. During prolonged heat, low humidity and very dry vegetation, the same ignition can develop into a fire requiring numerous appliances and many hours of firefighting.

Human behaviour therefore matters enormously. The Government cannot immediately cool the country, restore moisture to dried vegetation or remove weeks of accumulated heat from the landscape. It can, however, try to reduce avoidable sources of ignition. Disposable barbecues, bonfires, campfires, cigarettes, fireworks and other sources of heat can become much more consequential when the surrounding vegetation has effectively become fuel.

There is also a longer-term reason for taking the warning seriously. Britain is not becoming Spain, Greece or California overnight, and comparisons with those places can easily become exaggerated. Our climate, vegetation, housing patterns and emergency infrastructure are different. Nevertheless, the assumption that serious wildfire is an exotic problem belonging somewhere else is increasingly difficult to defend.

The UK has already experienced destructive moorland fires during previous hot summers, including the extensive Saddleworth Moor fires of 2018. For Rochdale this is not an abstract national concern. Moorland, grassland and countryside sit immediately beside settlements across the Pennine fringe, including areas around Littleborough, Wardle, Norden, Whitworth and the wider hills surrounding the borough. A serious moorland fire does not need to reach Rochdale town centre to affect Rochdale residents. Smoke, road closures, damaged habitats, exhausted emergency-service resources and threats to isolated properties can all spread consequences far beyond the flames themselves.

Climate science also points towards a future in which the weather conditions favourable to wildfire become more common. Research involving the Met Office and UK scientific institutions has concluded that human-caused climate change substantially increased the likelihood of the severe fire weather experienced during the 2022 heatwave. Climate-risk assessments anticipate more high fire-weather days as average temperatures rise, while longer periods of heat and drought can leave vegetation increasingly vulnerable to ignition.

That does not mean climate change can be blamed automatically for every individual fire. Fires still require ignition, fuel and conditions that allow them to spread. Land management, deliberate arson, accidental ignition and the speed of the emergency response all remain important. But the broader direction is difficult to ignore: a warmer climate can create more frequent periods in which an otherwise minor act of carelessness has much larger consequences.

This is why there is a sensible position between panic and dismissal. The Government should not turn the Emergency Alerts system into an electronic public-information poster. If the siren sounds too often for advice that is not genuinely urgent, its effectiveness may be weakened. Equally, a warning designed to prevent new fires during an already exceptional national wildfire situation is not obviously frivolous simply because no flames were visible from the recipient's window.

In fact, prevention may be one of the strongest arguments for using the system. Waiting until a wildfire is already moving towards houses means waiting until much of the opportunity to stop the emergency has disappeared. If a short national warning prevents even a small number of avoidable ignitions at a time when firefighters are already stretched, the intervention may prove proportionate despite its dramatic presentation.

The most interesting aspect of Friday's alert is therefore not the ten seconds of noise. It is what the noise was about. Britain has spent generations regarding wildfire principally as a rural inconvenience or an overseas catastrophe. Emergency planners are now treating it as a hazard capable of threatening homes, infrastructure and life on a sufficiently large scale to justify use of a national warning system.

For residents of Rochdale and the wider Pennine area, that deserves attention. Our landscape contains precisely the combination of moorland, grass, woodland and settlements that can make prolonged dry conditions problematic. The lesson is not that every warm weekend should cause millions of phones to scream. It is that the range of emergencies Britain prepares for may be changing.

If wetter summers return and warnings of this kind remain extremely rare, Friday's alert may ultimately be remembered as an unusually cautious intervention during an exceptional season. If periods of intense heat, drought and severe fire weather become more frequent, it may instead look like an early example of something the public later comes to regard as normal.

That is the uncomfortable possibility behind the alarm. The argument is not really about whether people were irritated by their phones. It is about whether Britain is entering a period in which hazards once considered unusual have to become part of ordinary civil protection.

Whether Friday's alert was perfectly calibrated is open to debate. The underlying wildfire risk is not.

articles.title: Littleborough residents help boost flood resilience through Resilient Roch project
articles.excerpt: Residents at Olive Standring House in Littleborough have joined housing, council and Environment Agency teams to refresh planters while highlighting ongoing flood-resilience work across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Residents at Olive Standring House in Littleborough have been enjoying the summer sunshine while playing a part in efforts to improve flood resilience in the borough.

Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, Rochdale Borough Council, the Environment Agency and contractors joined residents to refresh planters as part of the ongoing Resilient Roch project.

The programme is supporting homes affected by the devastating Boxing Day floods of 2015 as well as properties considered to remain at risk of flooding today.

The work at Olive Standring House provided an opportunity for residents to get involved in improvements to their surroundings while drawing attention to the wider measures being introduced to make homes and communities more resilient to future flooding.

Further improvements are being rolled out across the borough, including flood doors, sump pumps and flood barriers. These measures are intended to reduce the impact on individual properties when extreme rainfall and rising water levels threaten homes.

Littleborough and the wider Pennine area have first-hand experience of the disruption flooding can cause. The Boxing Day floods in 2015 affected communities across the borough and remain an important reference point for current flood-prevention and resilience work.

The Resilient Roch programme brings together housing providers, the council, the Environment Agency, contractors and residents, combining physical protection measures with work intended to help communities prepare for future flood events.

The planter work at Olive Standring House is a smaller but visible part of that wider programme, giving residents an opportunity to participate directly while improvements continue elsewhere across Rochdale borough.

articles.title: Are our reservoirs recovering after Rochdale's exceptionally dry summer?
articles.excerpt: North West reservoir stocks fell sharply during July, but the latest verified figures show the region entered the dry spell with considerably more water in storage than at the same point last year.
articles.content_html:
After weeks of heat, dry ground and remarkably little rainfall, attention is turning to the North West's reservoirs — and whether the return of more changeable weather has begun to undo the damage.

The short answer is: not yet, based on the latest reservoir figures Rochdale Daily has been able to verify — although the overall regional position remains considerably better than it was this time last year.

United Utilities publishes figures covering the major reservoir systems supplying the North West. For the week ending 19 July, total regional reservoir storage stood at 70.6%. That was down 4.1 percentage points in just one week and slightly below the 72.7% average for that point in the year.

Of particular interest to Rochdale are United Utilities' Pennine sources. These were at 64.3% capacity by 19 July, having fallen four percentage points in a week. The normal level for that point in the year is 66.6%.

There is some reassuring context. At the same point last year, the Pennine sources were at just 42.2%. That means that despite this summer's prolonged dry weather, Pennine storage remained more than 20 percentage points higher than during the equivalent week of 2025.

Haweswater and Thirlmere — enormously important components of the North West's water-supply system — stood at a combined 67%. That represented a fall of 4.7 percentage points in a week, although it remained above the 64% seasonal average and above last year's 60.3%. At Thirlmere itself, the water surface was recorded at 4.01 metres below top water level.

Across the major reservoir groups, regional storage was 70.6%, Pennine sources 64.3%, Haweswater and Thirlmere 67%, Dee and Vyrnwy 76.5%, and Carlisle 66.8%. Every major group recorded a weekly decline, with Carlisle falling nine percentage points in a week.

So will a few rainy days refill them? Unfortunately, reservoirs do not work quite that quickly. Rain falling onto Rochdale does not translate immediately into an equivalent rise in reservoir storage. After a prolonged dry spell, rainfall must interact with dry soils, vegetation, rivers and the wider catchment before significant quantities reach reservoirs, while homes and businesses continue using water every day.

This is why several genuinely wet periods — rather than a couple of showers — can be required before reservoir levels show a meaningful and sustained recovery. The North West also operates as an interconnected water-supply system, meaning Rochdale's water security cannot be judged simply by looking at the nearest reservoir and seeing how full it appears.

The dry conditions have accompanied an exceptionally hot start to summer. By the middle of July, England and Wales had each received only around 34% of their normal rainfall for the entire summer season, despite being halfway through meteorological summer. Some locations had recorded no measurable July rainfall at all by that point.

Temperatures have also been extraordinary. By 15 July, the UK had already experienced more days above 30C during 2026 than occurred during the whole of the famously hot summer of 1976.

The Environment Agency has consequently been closely monitoring water resources across England, while United Utilities was under enhanced monitoring and operations for its Haweswater and Carlisle water-resource zones during July. Wildfires across Greater Manchester, Cheshire and Derbyshire created additional pressure, with significant quantities of water also required for firefighting.

The figures require perspective. Storage has fallen substantially and the Pennine system was below its seasonal average in the latest verified snapshot, but this is not the same situation as last summer. Pennine sources being at 64.3% compared with 42.2% at the same point in 2025 gives the region considerably more resilience. Haweswater and Thirlmere were also above both their seasonal average and last year's level.

The key question now is what happens during August. Several weeks of regular rainfall could begin rebuilding water resources. A return to prolonged heat and dry weather, however, would place further pressure on reservoir stocks at precisely the time when summer water demand remains high.

For Rochdale residents looking at exposed reservoir banks and wondering whether recent rain means the problem is over, the answer is more complicated: the North West entered the dry spell with a healthier reserve than last year, but reservoir stocks have been falling quickly and recovery requires sustained rainfall rather than the occasional wet day.

Rochdale Daily will continue tracking reservoir levels as new figures are published.

articles.title: Residents furious as waste returns to Heywood alley weeks after major council clean-up
articles.excerpt: Residents say household waste has again been dumped in the alleyway linking Marlborough Street and Canal Street in Heywood, just weeks after council crews carried out a major clearance operation.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Heywood have expressed anger after rubbish was allegedly dumped again in an alleyway just weeks after council crews carried out a major clearance operation.

The alleyway connecting Marlborough Street and Canal Street had previously become heavily cluttered with waste, including discarded food, chairs, refrigerators and freezers. Residents said the accumulation was attracting significant numbers of vermin.

A few weeks ago, two large council vehicles were deployed to clear the alley and remove the accumulated rubbish.

Residents now say household bins have once again been emptied into the alleyway, raising fears that the vermin problem will return.

The repeated dumping is particularly frustrating for families during the summer months. People living nearby say children are being prevented from comfortably using their own backyards because of the rubbish and associated vermin.

One resident described the behaviour as 'extremely selfish, lazy and utterly disgusting' and said photographic evidence and CCTV footage would be submitted to Rochdale Borough Council and Greater Manchester Police.

Residents hope any available footage will help establish who is responsible and allow the relevant authorities to consider enforcement action. No individual has been identified by Rochdale Daily and no assumption should be made about responsibility unless supported by evidence and confirmed by the appropriate authority.

Fly-tipping and repeated waste dumping can create environmental and public-health problems beyond the appearance of an area, particularly where food waste provides a readily available source for rats and other vermin.

For residents who have already seen the alley cleared once, the message is that the community should not have to repeatedly bear the consequences of somebody else's waste.

Anyone with evidence relating to illegal dumping should preserve photographs or CCTV footage and report the matter through the appropriate council or police channels.

Nature lovers hoping to check in on the falcons at Rochdale Town Hall may have noticed that the popular live webcam is currently unavailable.

The camera has temporarily gone offline because of technical problems, but plans are already in place for a new camera to be installed.

The replacement will allow residents and wildlife enthusiasts to continue following the lives of the birds from Rochdale Town Hall, giving people a close-up view without disturbing them.

The webcam has provided an unusual window into urban wildlife in the heart of Rochdale, allowing viewers to observe the falcons from their phones and computers and helping to build interest in the birds living alongside the town centre.

Falcons and other birds of prey have increasingly made use of tall urban buildings, which can provide high nesting and roosting locations similar in some respects to the cliffs and elevated sites they use in the wild.

The temporary loss of the camera does not mean the birds themselves have disappeared; it is the webcam equipment that is affected.

A further update is expected within the next few days, including more information about the replacement camera and when viewers will once again be able to watch the falcons live.

articles.title: Comment: Rochdale Canal should be the jewel in the town's crown
articles.excerpt: Steven Parker of the Rochdale Canal Group argues that a living canal basin filled with boats, heritage, independent businesses and public space could bring visitors, jobs and regeneration to Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
This is a comment article by Steven Parker of the Rochdale Canal Group. The views expressed are his own.

Rochdale Branch Canal

Industrial units will not bring visitors to Rochdale, but a living canal basin filled with boats, a heritage centre, café, independent shops and exhibition space most definitely will.

Our historic canals should be the jewel in Rochdale's crown, but instead they languish neglected and forgotten.

The time is right for real change along the Rochdale Canal corridor, and we must be instrumental in making it happen.

A revitalised canal corridor has the potential to offer far more than an attractive waterside environment. Done properly, regeneration could create environmental improvements, attract visitors, support independent businesses, create employment and reconnect Rochdale with an extraordinary part of its industrial heritage.

A living canal basin would give people a reason to spend time in Rochdale rather than simply pass through it. Boats bring movement and activity. A heritage centre could tell the story of the canal and the industries it once served. Cafés, independent shops and exhibition spaces could provide places for residents and visitors to meet, spend money and experience something distinctive to the town.

Rochdale's industrial history should not simply be something remembered in photographs. The surviving canal corridor provides an opportunity to use that history as part of the borough's future.

Environmental, regenerative and job-creation opportunities will follow if Rochdale is ambitious enough to recognise the potential sitting alongside its historic waterways.

The opportunity is there. The question is whether Rochdale is prepared to take it.

Steven Parker Rochdale Canal Group Originally written 8 September 2024.

articles.title: Watching Wednesday's solar eclipse? The glasses you need to protect your eyes
articles.excerpt: Rochdale is preparing for Wednesday's major partial solar eclipse - but ordinary sunglasses are not safe. Here's what to look for in eclipse glasses and how to watch safely.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale is preparing for one of the most spectacular astronomical events visible from Britain in years, with a major partial solar eclipse due to darken the skies on Wednesday 12 August.

But anyone planning to look up needs to get one thing sorted before Wednesday evening: ordinary sunglasses are not safe for watching a solar eclipse.

Specialist solar-eclipse glasses are designed to reduce the Sun's radiation to a level suitable for direct viewing. The important marking to look for is ISO 12312-2, the international safety standard covering filters used for direct observation of the Sun.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich advises eclipse watchers to use purpose-made solar viewing protection. Eclipse glasses should be inspected before use and should not be used if the filter is scratched, torn, punctured or otherwise damaged.

WHAT SHOULD YOU BUY?

Rochdale Daily has found Astral Solar Eclipse Paper Glasses from Absolute Eclipse, designed specifically for direct solar viewing. The retailer states that the glasses comply with EN ISO 12312-2:2015 and use specialist solar-filter material.

Single pairs are advertised at approximately £4.30 based on the retailer's euro price and current exchange rates, although the exact sterling amount charged may vary with the exchange rate and payment provider. Multipacks are also available for families and groups.

BUY ASTRAL SOLAR ECLIPSE GLASSES: https://absoluteeclipse.eu/products/astral-solar-eclipse-paper-glasses?sca_ref=12037834.ocoapNfFOz&sca_source=Rochdaledaily

Rochdale Daily may receive a commission if readers purchase through the link above. This does not increase the price paid by the customer.

WHY AREN'T SUNGLASSES ENOUGH?

Even extremely dark conventional sunglasses are designed for everyday daylight, not staring directly at the Sun. During an eclipse, the reduction in visible daylight can also create a false sense that looking towards the Sun has become safer. It has not.

Looking directly at the Sun without appropriate protection can damage the retina at the back of the eye. Crucially, retinal injury may occur without immediate pain, meaning somebody may not realise damage has occurred while they are watching.

Purpose-made eclipse glasses meeting the appropriate solar-viewing standard or an indirect viewing method such as a pinhole projector should therefore be used.

CHECK YOUR GLASSES BEFORE PUTTING THEM ON

Before Wednesday's eclipse, check the solar-filter material carefully. If you find scratches, holes, tears, punctures or other damage, do not use that pair.

Put your eclipse glasses on before looking towards the Sun and turn away from the Sun before removing them. Children should be supervised to make sure the glasses remain correctly positioned while they are looking upwards.

There is another important distinction: eclipse glasses are intended for unaided viewing with your eyes. They should not be used to look through binoculars, telescopes or camera lenses. Optical equipment concentrates sunlight and requires correctly fitted specialist solar filters designed for that equipment.

WHAT IF YOU CAN'T GET GLASSES IN TIME?

You can still experience the eclipse without looking directly at the Sun. A simple pinhole projector allows sunlight to pass through a small opening and project an image of the partially eclipsed Sun onto another surface.

Whatever method you choose, do not improvise with ordinary sunglasses, tinted glass or homemade eye filters.

WHEN CAN ROCHDALE SEE IT?

The eclipse takes place on Wednesday 12 August, beginning in the early evening and reaching maximum coverage shortly after 7pm in the Greater Manchester area. Around nine-tenths of the Sun is expected to be obscured at maximum, weather permitting.

It should create an extraordinary sight across Rochdale - but the most important preparation is making sure everyone watching has suitable eye protection before looking towards the Sun.

articles.title: Rare partial solar eclipse will be visible over Rochdale on Wednesday
articles.excerpt: A major partial solar eclipse will be visible across the UK on Wednesday 12 August, with around nine-tenths of the Sun expected to be obscured from the Rochdale area if skies remain clear.
articles.content_html:
People across Rochdale will have the chance to see one of the most striking astronomical events visible from the UK in years when a partial solar eclipse takes place on Wednesday 12 August.

The Met Office says the extent of the Sun's coverage and the precise timing of maximum obscuration will vary across the country, while local cloud and weather conditions will determine how much people are actually able to see.

Across the UK the eclipse will be substantial. Northeast Scotland is expected to see around 88 per cent of the Sun covered shortly before 7pm, while the far southwest of England will see around 96 per cent coverage shortly after 7.15pm.

For Greater Manchester and Rochdale, the eclipse is expected to begin at around 6.13pm, reach maximum obscuration at approximately 7.10pm and finish shortly after 8pm. Around 90 per cent of the Sun is expected to be covered at maximum, although the exact figure varies slightly by location.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich says the 12 August eclipse will be the largest partial solar eclipse visible from the UK and Ireland since 1999.

WEATHER COULD MAKE OR BREAK THE VIEW

Even a major eclipse can disappear behind typical British cloud, so anyone hoping to watch it should check the latest local forecast on the day. Thin or broken cloud may still allow glimpses, while thicker cloud could block the event completely.

HOW TO WATCH SAFELY

The Met Office stresses that people must never look directly at the Sun. Ordinary sunglasses are not safe for viewing an eclipse.

Certified eclipse glasses designed specifically for direct solar viewing can be used if they are undamaged and meet the appropriate safety standard. Another safe option is a pinhole projector, which allows the Sun's image to be projected onto a surface without looking directly at it.

Cameras, binoculars and telescopes should never be pointed at the Sun unless they are fitted with specialist solar filters designed for the equipment. Looking through an optical device without suitable protection can cause severe and permanent eye injury.

For residents lucky enough to get clear skies, Wednesday evening should provide a rare opportunity to see daylight noticeably dim as the Moon passes across most of the Sun's disc.

Rochdale Daily will monitor the local forecast ahead of the eclipse and update readers if viewing conditions become clearer.

articles.title: Fresh complaints over persistent landfill odour as Heywood residents report 'sewer' stench and fly infestation
articles.excerpt: Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong foul odour and increasing numbers of flies, prompting renewed questions over the long-running issues surrounding the Pilsworth South landfill site.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong unpleasant smell drifting across parts of the town, with many describing an odour resembling sewage, rotting waste or landfill gas. The latest complaints have reignited concerns over the long-running issues surrounding the nearby Pilsworth South landfill site.

Several residents also reported unusually high numbers of flies, a problem which campaigners have previously associated with the landfill during earlier periods of odour complaints.

Rebecca Hodkinson wrote: "Yep... Unfortunately. And the amount of flies is something else this year."

Billy Casper added: "It stunk rotten like sewers when I was walking up Heywood past Iceland at 5.30 this evening. I don't think it was the landfill though."

Jeanette Noble commented: "I've been smelling it on Darnhill for a few months and the amount of flies is terrible."

Although some residents believe the smell may have originated elsewhere, the recurrence of similar complaints has led many to question whether problems linked to the landfill have returned.

The issue first gained widespread public attention during 2024 when thousands of complaints were submitted to the Environment Agency by residents across Heywood, Middleton, Bury and Rochdale. The smell became one of the borough's most significant environmental concerns, leading to regulatory investigations into landfill gas management and odour control measures at the site.

Under environmental law, landfill sites are permitted to operate only under an Environmental Permit issued by the Environment Agency. Operators are legally required to use Best Available Techniques (BAT) to prevent or minimise pollution, including offensive odours. Persistent smells escaping beyond the site boundary are not automatically unlawful, but they can lead to regulatory enforcement where permit conditions are breached. The Environment Agency has powers to require operational improvements, vary permit conditions, or take enforcement action where appropriate.

The issue has also attracted political attention. West Heywood councillor Angela Brown has repeatedly encouraged residents to report every odour incident directly to the Environment Agency, stressing that detailed reports help investigators establish patterns and build evidence. Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has likewise raised concerns publicly and in Parliament regarding the impact of the landfill on surrounding communities.

Controversy has continued following approval for further landfill operations despite ongoing complaints from nearby residents. Campaigners argue that expansion should not proceed until odour problems have been fully resolved, while regulators maintain that environmental permits require operators to comply with strict controls.

Residents experiencing offensive odours are encouraged to report incidents directly to the Environment Agency, recording the date, time, location, weather conditions and a description of the smell. Multiple reports from different locations can assist investigators in determining whether a wider environmental incident is occurring.

For many residents, the recurring nature of the complaints is becoming increasingly frustrating. While only a full investigation can determine the source of any individual odour event, the persistence of reports over recent years demonstrates that confidence among the local community has yet to be restored.

articles.title: Heat exposes challenges facing Rochdale workers and Britain’s ageing infrastructure
articles.excerpt: Temperatures are forecast to reach around 27°C in Rochdale today, while hotter conditions affect other parts of England. The weather is renewing questions about worker protection, climate change and whether Britain’s buildings and infrastructure are prepared for warmer summers.
articles.content_html:
Warm conditions are presenting renewed challenges for workers in Rochdale and across the country today, raising questions about whether climate change, inadequate infrastructure investment or a combination of both has left Britain poorly prepared for increasingly hot summers.

Temperatures in Rochdale are forecast to rise to approximately 27°C during the afternoon, with the hottest conditions expected between 3pm and 5pm. Although that is below the extreme temperatures recorded during previous heatwaves, it can still create difficult conditions inside poorly ventilated offices, factories, warehouses, workshops and vehicles.

Conditions are hotter in parts of southern and south-eastern England, where temperatures are significantly above those being experienced across Greater Manchester. The contrast means Britain is not facing identical conditions everywhere, but the national trend towards warmer and more frequent hot periods is placing increasing pressure on workplaces and public infrastructure.

Office workers can struggle in buildings with large windows, limited ventilation, sealed windows or insufficient cooling. Computers, lighting and large numbers of people can raise indoor temperatures beyond those recorded outside, leaving employees dealing with fatigue, headaches, dehydration and reduced concentration.

The risks are greater for people undertaking strenuous or outdoor work. Construction workers, roofers, landscapers, refuse collectors, delivery drivers, road crews, agricultural workers and utility engineers may be required to perform physically demanding tasks in direct sunlight while wearing heavy clothing or protective equipment.

Heat stress can develop when the body is unable to regulate its temperature effectively. Symptoms can include tiredness, dizziness, confusion, headaches, excessive sweating, muscle cramps and nausea. More serious cases can lead to heat exhaustion or heatstroke, requiring urgent medical attention.

There is no fixed maximum legal workplace temperature in Britain. The Health and Safety Executive says this is because workplaces vary considerably, with some industries naturally operating in hotter environments. Employers must nevertheless comply with health and safety law, maintain a reasonable working temperature, provide clean and fresh air and assess risks to employees.

For outdoor and physically demanding roles, sensible precautions can include access to drinking water, additional breaks, shaded rest areas, lighter clothing where safety permits and rescheduling the hardest work away from the hottest part of the day. Employers may also need to monitor staff for signs of heat stress and allow workers time to become accustomed to unusually warm conditions.

Whether Britain’s difficulties can be blamed on government underinvestment or climate change is not an either-or question.

Human-driven climate change is increasing the likelihood and severity of hot weather in Britain. Official figures published by the Office for National Statistics show that the average number of hot days during the decade from 2015 to 2024 was nearly double that recorded between 2005 and 2014. The most recent decade was also warmer than previous reference periods.

However, climate change does not explain why so many British workplaces, schools, hospitals, homes and transport systems struggle when temperatures rise. Much of the country’s built environment was designed for a historically cooler climate, while investment in ventilation, shading, insulation, urban trees and other forms of heat adaptation has not consistently kept pace with the changing risk.

The Climate Change Committee has repeatedly warned that Britain is inadequately prepared for the effects of a warmer climate. Its 2026 assessment said hotter heatwaves could eventually cause the overwhelming majority of existing homes to overheat without sufficient adaptation. Although that warning focused primarily on housing, many of the same construction and ventilation problems affect workplaces.

Successive governments of different political parties have therefore inherited and contributed to the problem. Britain’s exposure has developed over decades through ageing buildings, inconsistent adaptation policies and a planning system that has not always treated overheating as a central design concern.

The economic consequences are also significant. Experimental analysis by the Office for National Statistics estimated that hot days caused an average annual productivity loss of approximately £1.2 billion between 1998 and 2021, even after accounting for adaptation. Workers generally complete tasks more slowly in excessive heat, while employers may face disruption, additional breaks, equipment problems and higher cooling costs.

Urban areas can be particularly vulnerable because roads, roofs, concrete and other hard surfaces absorb heat during the day and release it slowly. Trees, parks, rivers and other green or blue spaces provide natural cooling, but their availability varies considerably between communities.

The challenge facing the Government is therefore twofold. Reducing greenhouse-gas emissions remains necessary to limit the severity of future warming, but adaptation is also required because some further climate change is already unavoidable.

That means improving building standards, retrofitting unsuitable properties, expanding tree cover, protecting green space and ensuring schools, hospitals, care facilities, transport networks and workplaces can remain safe during hot weather. Employers must also recognise that heat planning can no longer be treated as an exceptional response reserved for record-breaking temperatures.

Today’s weather in Rochdale is warm rather than unprecedented. Nevertheless, it provides another indication of a challenge that will become increasingly familiar. Climate change is making hot periods more likely, while inadequate preparation determines how disruptive and dangerous those periods become.

The evidence suggests both factors are responsible. The climate is changing, but Britain’s failure to adapt its workplaces and infrastructure quickly enough is increasing the burden placed on office staff, labourers and those whose jobs cannot simply be moved into an air-conditioned room.

articles.title: Discover the beauty on your doorstep: The spectacular walks of Shawclough and Healey
articles.excerpt: From Healey Dell to the Pennine moors, Shawclough and Healey offer some of Greater Manchester's finest walking routes. Here's how to enjoy them responsibly while discovering the wildlife and landscapes on your doorstep.
articles.content_html:
With rolling moorland, ancient woodland, dramatic valleys and panoramic Pennine views, Shawclough and Healey offer some of the finest walking routes anywhere in Greater Manchester. Just a few minutes from Rochdale town centre, the area provides easy access to miles of public footpaths, bridleways and countryside that attract walkers, runners, cyclists and nature lovers throughout the year.

Whether you're looking for a gentle afternoon stroll or a challenging hike onto the South Pennine moors, there is a route to suit every ability. Healey Dell Nature Reserve remains one of the area's most popular destinations, with its historic railway viaduct, woodland trails and the River Spodden winding through a picturesque valley rich in wildlife. From there, walkers can continue towards Shawclough, Rooley Moor Road, Brown Wardle Hill, Knowl Hill and the Pennine Bridleway, enjoying some of the most impressive views across Rochdale, Rossendale and beyond. The wider area also links into the Rochdale Way and Rossendale Way, providing opportunities for much longer circular walks.

The landscape changes dramatically with the seasons. During late summer, the surrounding moorland is coloured by flowering heather, while ancient dry stone walls, reservoirs and grazing farmland create the classic Pennine scenery that has inspired walkers for generations.

The area is also a haven for wildlife. At this time of year, walkers are likely to spot kestrels hovering above the fields, buzzards circling on thermals, swallows and house martins feeding before beginning their autumn migration, and flocks of goldfinches gathering on seed heads. In the woodlands around Healey Dell, visitors may hear great spotted woodpeckers, nuthatches, wrens, robins and tawny owls after dusk. Lucky walkers may even catch sight of kingfishers along quieter stretches of the River Spodden. Roe deer are regularly seen at dawn and dusk around Healey Dell, Rooley Moor and neighbouring farmland, while foxes, badgers, rabbits and brown hares also inhabit the surrounding countryside.

As enjoyable as these walks are, visitors are reminded that much of the surrounding countryside remains working farmland. Public Rights of Way allow people to cross private land using designated footpaths and bridleways, but walkers should always remain on the marked route unless they are on land with wider access rights. Respecting the Countryside Code helps ensure these routes remain open for everyone to enjoy.

Simple acts of courtesy make a significant difference. Gates should always be left exactly as they are found. If a gate is closed, close it again after passing through. If it has been left open, leave it open. Farmers often manage livestock carefully, and an incorrectly opened or closed gate can allow animals to stray or separate livestock.

Dog owners also have an important responsibility. Even the friendliest dog can frighten livestock, particularly sheep with lambs or cattle with calves. Dogs should be kept under close control and, wherever livestock are present, they should be kept on a lead. If cattle become inquisitive or begin approaching, it is usually safest to release the dog if necessary, as it can outrun livestock and return once the danger has passed.

Walkers are also encouraged to remain vigilant for injured or distressed animals. If you discover a sheep that has rolled onto its back and cannot get up—a situation known as being 'cast' or 'turned over'—or encounter injured cattle, the best course of action is to contact the farmer if they can be identified, or report the location to the local authority or police if there is an immediate welfare concern. Unless you are experienced and it is safe to do so, avoid attempting to handle large livestock yourself.

The natural beauty of Shawclough and Healey depends on everyone doing their part. Taking litter home, avoiding lighting fires, respecting wildlife and staying on established paths all help protect this special landscape for future generations.

For many residents, one of the greatest pleasures of living in Rochdale is having countryside of this quality virtually on the doorstep. In less than an hour, it is possible to walk from peaceful woodland to open Pennine moorland, passing historic landmarks, abundant wildlife and breathtaking viewpoints along the way.

As summer gradually gives way to autumn, there are few better times to lace up your walking boots, head for the hills and rediscover the remarkable countryside that surrounds Shawclough and Healey.
